opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on the time horizon, and the short-run and long-run pictures can look quite different.

In the near term, as AI systems become capable of doing a growing fraction of tasks but not all of them, I'd actually expect human wages to rise on average. The reason is complementarity. If AI automates some tasks in a production process, the remaining tasks that only humans can do become bottlenecks, and bottlenecks get more valuable. Overall output goes up a lot because of the automation, and the human labor that remains essential captures part of that gain. So you could see a period where wages for many workers grow faster than they have in decades, even while specific occupations get disrupted and some people face real hardship in transition.

The long run is where it gets more uncomfortable. If you eventually get AI systems that can do essentially everything a human worker can do, including physical tasks once robotics catches up, then human labor stops being a bottleneck. At that point the wage a human can command is roughly capped by the cost of running an AI or robot that does the same job. And that cost could keep falling as compute gets cheaper and models get more efficient. Labor would become like any other input that has a cheap substitute, so its price converges toward the cost of that substitute. That could plausibly be below what a person needs to live on, in which case wages would fall, potentially quite far, even as the economy as a whole becomes enormously richer.

So the picture I have is something like a rise and then a fall: wages going up for a while as AI complements human work, and then eventually declining once AI can substitute for humans across the board. The exact timing is very uncertain, it depends on how fast capabilities progress, how quickly compute scales, and how long the physical and robotics side lags behind cognitive work.

I'd add that falling wages wouldn't necessarily mean people are poorer. If the economy grows explosively, people who own capital, or who receive income through taxation and redistribution of that output, could be far better off than today. But it does mean that the traditional link between working and earning a living would weaken substantially, and income would increasingly come from ownership or transfers rather than labor. That's a big societal shift, and I think it's worth thinking seriously now about how we want to handle it, rather than assuming wages will just keep rising the way they have through past waves of technology.

r001.rationale: The response attributes long-run wage declines to AI becoming a cheap substitute for human labor, but does not identify diminishing returns to scaling AI workers.

r002.rationale: It says AI automation raises output and makes remaining human tasks more valuable, but does not clearly identify increased human productivity as a countervailing force to wage pressure from AI competition.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on the time horizon, and the dynamics are different in the short run versus the long run.

In the short run, my expectation is actually that wages go up. The reason is that AI systems are going to be imperfect substitutes for human workers for a while. They'll automate some tasks but not others, and when you automate part of a production process, the parts that still require humans become more valuable, because the whole process is now more productive. This is roughly what happened historically with automation: machines took over a lot of tasks, but the complementary human tasks got bid up, and wages rose enormously over the past two centuries. There's also a general equilibrium effect where AI makes the economy richer overall, capital accumulates faster, and that raises the marginal product of whatever labor is still needed. So in that early phase, I'd expect a fairly broad-based wage increase, even if specific occupations get hit hard.

The long run is where it gets more uncertain, and where I think people's intuitions from history can mislead them. Once AI systems can do essentially everything a human can do, and do it at a cost that's lower than what it takes to sustain a human, then the economic logic changes. At that point humans are competing directly with a form of labor that can be reproduced by building more hardware, and the price of that labor is going to be anchored to the cost of compute and energy, not to human subsistence. If compute keeps getting cheaper, which I expect, then the wage a human can command for doing work falls toward that compute cost, and that can end up well below what people need to live on.

So the picture I have is something like: wages rise, possibly quite a lot, during the transition, and then at some point they peak and start declining as substitution overtakes complementarity. When that peak happens is really hard to call. It depends on how fast capabilities improve, how quickly the physical capital stock can be scaled, and how much residual demand there is for things that specifically require a human, like certain kinds of services where people care that a person is involved.

One thing I'd emphasize is that falling wages doesn't automatically mean people are worse off. In a world where AI has made the economy vastly larger, the total output is enormous, and the question becomes who owns the capital and how the returns get distributed. If people hold assets, or if there's some redistribution mechanism, then living standards can keep rising even as labor income shrinks to almost nothing. So the key variable in the long run is less about wages and more about ownership and political arrangements. Wages are just a bad proxy for welfare once labor stops being the main input.

r001.rationale: The response says wages fall as AI becomes a cheaper direct substitute for human labor, but does not identify diminishing returns from scaling up AI workers as a cause.

r002.rationale: It explains that automating some tasks makes remaining human work more valuable and raises labor’s marginal product, counteracting wage pressure from substitution.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends a lot on how capable the AI workers are and how easily you can produce more of them. Initially, you could see human wages rise, even substantially, because AI makes people more productive. If you automate some tasks, you increase the demand for the complementary tasks that humans still do.

But that doesn’t necessarily continue indefinitely. If AI can do essentially everything a human worker can do, then firms have an alternative to hiring humans. And if the supply of AI labor can expand cheaply, that puts downward pressure on wages. Humans might still have jobs, but the wage at which employing them makes economic sense could be much lower.

The important distinction is between wages and income overall. You could have a much richer economy, with much cheaper goods and services, while the share of income going to human labor falls dramatically. Whether people benefit in that world depends a lot on who owns the capital and how the gains are distributed.

So I wouldn’t expect a simple story where wages either rise or fall throughout. You could get an initial period of rising wages followed by a reversal as AI becomes a sufficiently general substitute for human labor. The timing and magnitude of that reversal are much harder to predict.

r001.rationale: The response says cheaply expanding AI labor puts downward pressure on human wages, but it does not identify diminishing returns as the reason.

r002.rationale: The response says AI makes people more productive and can increase demand for tasks humans still perform, counteracting downward wage pressure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends quite a lot on the time horizon. Initially, AI can make human workers more productive, and that can increase wages. If you automate some of the tasks that people do, but you still need people for other tasks, then expanding production increases demand for the people who do those remaining tasks.

But I wouldn’t extrapolate that indefinitely. If AI workers become substitutes for humans across essentially the whole range of economically useful tasks, then you have a new source of labor whose supply can expand much more quickly than the human population. At that point, it becomes difficult for human workers to command high wages just on the basis of their labor.

The important distinction is between wages and income. You could have an economy that’s vastly richer while human wages fall. People might still have high incomes through ownership of capital or redistribution, but that’s a separate question from whether employers are willing to pay much for their work.

So my expectation would be that there can be a period where wages rise, potentially substantially, followed by downward pressure as AI becomes a sufficiently good substitute. How long that transition lasts depends on how quickly capabilities improve and how quickly we can deploy AI workers.

r001.rationale: The response says AI labor could substitute for humans and expand faster than the human population, putting downward pressure on wages. It does not identify diminishing returns as the reason.

r002.rationale: The response says AI can make human workers more productive, which can increase wages and counterbalance automation pressure while people remain needed for other tasks.
